message.content:
**Hydrogen – A Quick Reference to Its Key Properties**

| Category | Property | Value / Description |
|----------|----------|---------------------|
| **Basic Atomic Data** | Atomic number | 1 |
| | Atomic mass (average) | 1.008 u |
| | Electron configuration | 1s¹ |
| | Isotopes | ¹H (protium), ²H (deuterium), ³H (tritium) |
| | Natural abundance | ¹H ≈ 99.98 %, ²H ≈ 0.02 %, ³H negligible |
| | Ionization energy | 13.598 eV (first ionization) |
| | Electron affinity | –0.754 eV (negative, so H⁻ is unstable in gas phase) |
| | Electronegativity (Pauling) | 2.20 |
| | Atomic radius | ~53 pm (covalent) |
| **Physical State (at 25 °C, 1 atm)** | Phase | Gas |
| | Boiling point | –252.87 °C |
| | Melting point | –259.16 °C |
| | Density | 0.08988 g L⁻¹ |
| | Molar volume | 22.414 L mol⁻¹ |
| | Specific heat (gas) | 14.304 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ |
| | Thermal conductivity | 0.180 W m⁻¹ K⁻¹ |
| | Viscosity | 8.76 × 10⁻⁶ Pa s |
| | Sound speed | ~1270 m s⁻¹ |
| **Chemical Behavior** | Oxidation state | +1 (most common) |
| | Common compounds | H₂O, H₂SO₄, HCl, NH₃, CH₄, etc. |
| | Bonding | Forms covalent bonds; can form diatomic H₂, hydrides (ionic or covalent). |
| | Reactivity | Highly reactive with many elements; forms hydrides with metals, halogens, etc. |
| | Combustion | 2 H₂ + O₂ → 2 H₂O (exothermic, ΔH ≈ –286 kJ mol⁻¹) |
| | Redox behavior | Can act as both reducing and oxidizing agent depending on conditions. |
| **Isotopic Variants** | Protium (¹H) | Stable, most abundant. |
| | Deuterium (²H) | Stable, heavier isotope; used in nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) and as a tracer. |
| | Tritium (³H) | Radioactive (β‑emitter, half‑life ≈ 12.32 y); used in nuclear fusion research and as a tracer. |
| **Physical Constants** | Speed of light in vacuum | 299,792,458 m s⁻¹ |
| | Planck constant | 6.62607015 × 10⁻³⁴ J s |
| | Avogadro constant | 6.02214076 × 10²³ mol⁻¹ |
| | Boltzmann constant | 1.380649 × 10⁻²³ J K⁻¹ |
| **Role in Nature & Technology** | Stellar fusion | H + H → D + e⁺ + ν_e (proton–proton chain) |
| | Energy source | Hydrogen fusion powers stars; potential fusion fuel on Earth. |
| | Fuel cell chemistry | H₂ + ½ O₂ → H₂O (electrochemical energy conversion). |
| | Water formation | 2 H₂ + O₂ → 2 H₂O (key for life). |
| | Atmospheric composition | Minor component (~0.000055 % by volume on Earth). |
| | Industrial uses | Production of ammonia (Haber process), methanol, hydrogenation reactions, etc. |
| **Safety & Handling** | Flammability | Extremely flammable; explosive limits 4–75 % in air. |
| | Toxicity | Non‑toxic, but can cause asphyxiation in confined spaces. |
| | Storage | Requires high‑pressure cylinders or cryogenic tanks; can be stored as liquid at –253 °C. |

---

### Quick Takeaways

- **Hydrogen is the simplest element**: one proton, one electron, and (in its most common form) one neutron.
- **It exists mainly as a diatomic gas (H₂)** under normal conditions, but it can also be found as a monatomic ion (H⁺) in plasma or as a hydride (H⁻) in ionic compounds.
- **Its isotopes** (protium, deuterium, tritium) give it unique roles in nuclear physics, chemistry, and biology.
- **Hydrogen’s reactivity** makes it a cornerstone of organic and inorganic chemistry, as well as a key player in energy technologies such as fuel cells and potential fusion reactors.
- **Safety**: While non‑toxic, hydrogen’s high flammability and low density require careful handling and proper ventilation.

Feel free to ask if you’d like deeper details on any specific aspect—e.g., quantum mechanical properties, spectroscopic signatures, or industrial processes!
